text: So this is a talk about compute markets, but it's kind of more of a talk about why to make a compute market. If you don't know me, I'm Evan. We run a company called San Francisco Compute. We make a physically settled forwards market. So if you were here for the last talk, the last talk was basically why all the operators of GPU clusters don't really work very well. When we say physically settled, we mean we're the operator. We're both the operator of the hardware in the same way that a cloud is the operator of the hardware, and then we're also the market at the same time. It's kind of like a grid for compute. So the general gist of this is that in order to run and operate a supercomputer, we think problems start right at the design of the supercomputer, right in the design of the bill of materials. It's control of the backplane fabric as well. It's also control of bare metal orchestration. It's also services on top, VMs, and so on. There's a lot of different parts of the stack that you have to do effectively. Otherwise, the folks who have a data center and would like to make more money on that data center by becoming the GPU cloud end up failing for the customer. So that's what we do. We offer what's called supercomputing as a service. We go to folks who want to become a cloud. That's like folks who want to become what NVIDIA would call an NCP, or venture firms that want to have clusters for their portfolio and want to be able to reallocate that capacity when a company like Instinct is taking off, or AI companies who would like the residual value on the compute because they've realized that's really important to their financials but don't want to operate a supercomputer. So that's physical settlement. And then on top of that, we run a live order book for capacity that you can buy reserved either right now or in the future. This together is not at all what we thought we were going to be doing. Originally, we were this company called Junelark that was trying to make kind of like Suno or UDO, but prior to Suno or UDO. At the time, what you needed to do to realistically start Outlab was you needed to raise a big deposit, a huge one, which was $10 million at the time. We thought that was a crazy amount of money, and so we thought, no, that's stupid. We're going to raise 500K, and obviously what we're going to do is we're going to rent from somebody else. Obviously today, it's not $10 million. It's a billion dollars. And nonetheless, we had raised our 500K. We buy a big cluster, and then we're underwater on our cluster every month. And if we didn't sublease our cluster, we would have gone bankrupt. So if you've heard of GPU brokers, we were the first GPU broker because we were forced into being a GPU broker, so the first year of the company, it was us just trying to sell our cluster. Otherwise, we would go bankrupt. So I would wander around with these actual pieces of paper at NeurIPS, which both say H100 and A100 at the same time, because that's how I made the poster so quickly. And so this talk is not really about necessarily how a compute market works. It's how a compute market gets to exist. We like to think about it like there's this pamphlet, and on the pamphlet, on the front side, it's like, man, starting a Neolab sucks, there's all these different financial and economic problems. On the back of the pamphlet, it says compute markets. It's not super clear how one gets to the other until you open the pamphlet, and then like, holy shit, there's so much stuff in this pamphlet, and it keeps going, and there's so many folds. It's just a very difficult and challenging problem, because you need to solve two miracle problems to get working. You have to both make a market, which is a uniquely difficult problem, because it has a cold start problem. You also have to build a cloud, and then you have to not become a cloud, which is a whole separate challenge. But these are the problems that the labs are facing, and it's about to be the problems that everyone is about to facing. So if you work at a startup, these are your problems now. Right now, everybody is sold out of compute. This is probably not going to change for a while. So that means that you're going to have to buy a new cluster, a net new one, and there's a lead time. You have no way to pay for that cluster to come online now. You're going to pay for it to come online later. There's nothing in the market that can realistically get that cluster online for you now. Meanwhile, you're going to pay your entire bank balance as a deposit. The reason you're paying your entire bank balance as a deposit is because the lender has no idea how to underwrite AGI. How in the world are you supposed to do that? You've got two-person startups in San Francisco, or maybe New York, who say, I'm going to build super intelligence. No lender knows how to underwrite super intelligence. So they have no idea what the asset is worth. Meanwhile, your cluster is very likely to be delayed. That's because the lender needed to underwrite against the credit risk of the customer, and so they needed to know who was the customer first before you deploy the cluster. So right when the customer signs is the riskiest point in the entire operation. You wanted it to be the case that you built the cluster first, and then you sell it. This also helps reduce all sorts of different types of problems where clusters break. Meanwhile, most of the people who are setting up clusters are people who have the actual asset that makes the thing cheap. Like you've got the data center space already. What that doesn't get is supercomputing expertise, as we saw in the last talk, if you've watched that one. Meanwhile, you're going to run into the exact same problem that Junelark did, which is you're going to either way overbuy or you're going to way underbuy. That's because AI doesn't have margins that look like SaaS companies, and so you don't have very much margin for error, and so the chances that you either underbuy and somebody else wins because they did it correctly, or you overbuy and then you just become stability AI or you blow up, you end up like character AI, are really high. So these are all the same problem. They're all just different types of risk. They're technical risk. They're financial risk. They're credit risk. They're all one big bundled risk problem, which is the problem that we end up solving, and it's also the problem that we think compute markets broadly the entire industry solves. So we'll walk through each one of these and walk how that gets to a compute market, because if you don't understand these, it's kind of unclear why you would want a compute market, and they almost seem like this problem that somebody thinks, oh, wow, compute markets are cool, so I'm going to go start one. We think they should be derived from the actual problems that people face, which is, first, everyone is sold out. Why are they sold out? Because the lender couldn't finance the cluster unless you had a long-term offtake agreement. In CPUs, this wasn't the case, because CPU buyers are SaaS companies. SaaS companies have high margins, and because they have high margins, you can build a product that rewards you for having a great that rewards you with high margins for your CPUs. Think about it like this way. If you're a SaaS company and your underlying cloud doubles their prices, you don't go bankrupt. You hate your cloud, you're mad, but you don't go bankrupt. If you're an AI company and your underlying cloud doubles their prices, you go bankrupt unless you go to some other underlying cloud. And what that means is that you're actually price sensitive, and because you're actually price sensitive, and there's nothing keeping you at any particular cloud, so you can't sell on demand because your customers will immediately leave to whoever is cheaper. And so that means that in order to finance GPU clusters, you have to have long-term take-or-pay contracts, hopefully with someone who has investment-grade credit. However, if you don't have liquidity on those, if you're selling reserved and your customer can't get out, then that also means that some other customer who wants the capacity right now because their instinct and their product is taking off can't pay for anything. They have to finance a new cluster, which has a lead time, because the physical world just exists and it's going to take a while. Sometimes you even have to build the damn data center. And then, because you're financing a new cluster, you're going to pay a deposit, because almost nobody in AI has any reasonable credit. And because this is a brand-new technology, all these companies are new, meanwhile, even as you start to scale up that ladder, you're still going to run into credit issues all the way through. It's the number one bottleneck of AI at the moment. It's not power. You hit credit way before you hit AI, or way before you hit power. So what that means is every inference company, every Neolab, they're bottlenecked by how much cash do they have in the bank account. And so they go back to the venture capitalist, who says, oh, I'm going to fund at the model layer, the application layer, the inference layer, because I don't want to fund all of that CapEx stuff. And so the venture capitalist then funds all the CapEx stuff by giving the new Neolab or new inference company the check that they then send to the cloud, which is the deposit for the cluster. And that's how you underwrite the customer. So the clusters then are delayed, because the cloud couldn't actually deploy the cluster until they had the customer in hand. And so that was the riskiest point. So therefore, what should have happened was the cloud had bought the cluster ahead of time, and then waited until it was landed in the data center, and then sold it. And that means you have way less likelihood of delays. Meanwhile, the cluster is very likely to break when you get the cluster as the customer, because you don't have liquidity. And so if the failure rate is higher than what you expect, and you don't have the ability to transition a node in, then you don't have anywhere you can pull nodes from, which means that if you need new nodes to make up for the failed ones, you have to RMA them, which means you have to get a new node. And then that gets us back to several steps before, where you have the lead time problem again. And so everything breaks for everybody all the time. Once you have gotten through all of that as a new AI lab, your problems are, like everyone was sold out, you then had to wait a little bit.
